units.title: Unit 61 — Motion: taking steps
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 128–129 (PDF pages 130–131).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · movement, crowds and metaphorical progress
learningObjectives: Distinguish subtle meanings of verbs for walking, unsteady movement and pursuit.
Interpret figurative movement verbs describing progress, failure and personal resilience.
Describe the movement of groups using water-related verbs and their different implications.
Choose accurate metaphorical step collocations and recognise additional walking verbs from the exercises.

sectionsChecked: A · Verbs of movement, table and usage contrasts
C · Water-related verbs applied to people
D · Metaphorical steps and Common mistakes box

items.pt: mancar; andar com dificuldade
items.example: After injuring his ankle, the researcher limped across the laboratory.
items.note: An uneven walk caused by pain or injury, often affecting one leg.

items.pt: saltitar; pular em um pé só
items.example: The athlete hopped on one foot to test whether her ankle was stable.
items.note: Moving by jumping on one foot, or with both feet briefly leaving the ground in animals such as rabbits.

items.pt: cambalear; andar sem equilíbrio
items.example: He staggered towards the exit after becoming dizzy in the heat.
items.note: Unsteady movement, often because of illness, alcohol or extreme tiredness.

items.pt: tropeçar; dar um passo em falso
items.example: She stumbled over a loose paving stone but managed not to fall.
items.note: Nearly fall after tripping or losing your footing; also used figuratively for hesitant progress.

items.pt: mover-se de modo brusco e descontrolado; dar um solavanco
items.example: The ferry lurched sideways when a powerful wave struck it.
items.note: A sudden, uncontrolled movement, especially on unstable transport or when unsteady.

items.pt: andar na ponta dos pés
items.example: He tiptoed past the bedroom so as not to disturb the sleeping child.
items.note: Move quietly on the front of your feet to avoid being heard.

items.pt: caminhar sem pressa; passear tranquilamente
items.example: We ambled through the old quarter without a fixed destination.
items.note: Walk at an easy, unhurried pace, usually for pleasure.

items.pt: caminhar com passos largos e decididos
items.example: The director strode into the meeting room and announced the decision.
items.note: Walk with long, confident, purposeful steps; past tense strode.

items.pt: andar de modo arrogante ou exibido; desfilar
items.example: He strutted around the office as though the promotion were entirely his achievement.
items.note: Walk in an exaggerated, self-important way; often critical.

items.pt: caminhar pesadamente por um longo período
items.example: The hikers tramped across the muddy fields for hours.
items.note: Walk with firm, heavy steps, often over a long distance.

items.pt: pisotear; esmagar com os pés
items.example: Visitors had trampled the delicate plants near the footpath.
items.note: Step repeatedly or heavily on something, often causing damage; unlike tramp, takes an object.

items.pt: bater o pé com força; pisar com força
items.example: The child stamped his feet when told that the game was over.
items.note: Bring a foot down forcefully, often to show irritation; British English uses stamp here.

items.pt: caminhar arrastando os pés e com esforço
items.example: Exhausted volunteers trudged back to the shelter in the pouring rain.
items.note: Move slowly and heavily because of fatigue or difficult conditions.

items.pt: perseguir; correr atrás de
items.example: Security staff chased the intruder through the station.
items.note: Move quickly in pursuit of someone or something with the aim of catching it.

items.pt: chegar a um fim pouco satisfatório; terminar sem vigor
items.example: The negotiations limped to a conclusion without resolving the central dispute.
items.note: Figurative limp suggests slow, weak or disappointing progress.

items.pt: descer rapidamente de um veículo
items.example: We can hop off at the next stop and walk along the river.
items.note: Informal, quick way to describe getting off a bus or similar transport.

items.pt: continuar aos trancos e barrancos; seguir com dificuldades
items.example: The small business staggered on despite months of falling revenue.
items.note: Continue functioning with difficulty rather than collapsing immediately.

items.pt: surpreendentemente; de modo impressionante
items.example: The new equipment proved staggeringly expensive to maintain.
items.note: An intensifier suggesting an astonishing or unexpectedly large degree.

items.word: lurch from one crisis to the next
items.pt: passar descontroladamente de uma crise para outra
items.example: The organisation lurched from one funding crisis to the next.
items.note: Suggests a lack of steady planning or control, not smooth progress.

items.pt: lidar com algo com naturalidade; encarar sem se abalar
items.example: She took the unexpected criticism in her stride and revised the proposal.
items.note: Accept a setback or difficulty calmly without letting it disrupt you.

items.pt: destruir ou desrespeitar os sonhos de alguém
items.example: A good mentor offers criticism without trampling on a student's dreams.
items.note: Figurative trample on means disregard or crush something valued by another person.

items.pt: cobrar insistentemente alguém por um pagamento
items.example: The accounts team had to chase several clients for overdue invoices.
items.note: Figurative chase means repeatedly contact someone to obtain something owed; it does not mean physically pursue them.

items.pt: tentativas hesitantes; primeiros esforços inseguros
items.example: Her stumbling attempts at public speaking gradually became more confident.
items.note: Stumbling describes hesitant, uneven early efforts rather than literal tripping.

items.pt: fluir; circular de modo contínuo
items.example: After the barriers were removed, pedestrians flowed steadily through the square.
items.note: Smooth, continuous movement resembling the movement of water.

items.pt: sair em grande número e de modo desordenado
items.example: When the concert ended, the audience spilled out onto the pavement.
items.note: A sudden movement outward, often in several directions and with little control.

items.pt: entrar em fluxo contínuo; afluir
items.example: Delegates streamed into the conference centre before the keynote speech.
items.note: A substantial number moving continuously in a fairly consistent direction.

items.pt: afluir em grande quantidade; entrar aos montes
items.example: Supporters poured into the city centre after the announcement.
items.note: Emphasises large numbers arriving continuously or from several directions.

items.pt: um pequeno fluxo de pessoas; pessoas chegando aos poucos
items.example: By mid-morning, only a trickle of visitors had reached the gallery.
items.note: A small and scattered number of people, unlike a continuous stream or large crowd.

items.pt: perambular sem rumo; fazer um percurso sinuoso
items.example: We meandered through the market, stopping whenever something caught our attention.
items.note: Follow a winding route or wander without a definite aim; also used for rivers.

items.pt: atravessar em massa; espalhar-se em grande número
items.example: Thousands of demonstrators flooded across the central square.
items.note: Suggests a very large number spreading rapidly across an area.

items.pt: dar um passo; tomar uma medida
items.example: The committee agreed to take a step towards greater transparency.
items.note: In figurative uses, take a step means act or make progress; do not substitute footsteps.

items.pt: dar um passo para trás; sofrer um retrocesso
items.example: Cutting the research budget would be a backward step for the programme.
items.note: Suggests regression or undoing earlier progress, rather than literal walking backwards.

items.pt: dar um passo decisivo
items.example: The regulator took a decisive step by requiring independent safety checks.
items.note: An action that strongly influences what happens next.

items.pt: dar uma medida crucial
items.example: Securing ethical approval was a critical step in the research process.
items.note: Critical means essential to progress, not necessarily a step involving criticism.

items.pt: dar o primeiro passo
items.example: Contacting the potential supervisor was her first step towards a doctorate.
items.note: The initial action in a longer process.

items.pt: dar um passo gigantesco; avançar muito
items.example: The discovery represented a giant step towards more reliable energy storage.
items.note: An especially large or important advance.

items.pt: dar um grande passo; tomar medida importante
items.example: The partners took a major step towards formalising their cooperation.
items.note: Major highlights the scale or importance of the action.

items.pt: dar um passo significativo
items.example: Publishing the findings was a significant step towards wider recognition.
items.note: An important, meaningful advance, without necessarily being decisive.

items.pt: tomar uma medida sem precedentes
items.example: The board took an unprecedented step by publishing the full internal review.
items.note: Unprecedented means not previously done in that context.

items.pt: entrar em fila, um atrás do outro
items.example: Students filed into the auditorium in near silence.
items.note: Enter in an orderly sequence, one person after another.

items.pt: passear com passos tranquilos e confiantes
items.example: They sauntered along the seafront after lunch.
items.note: Walk in a relaxed, leisurely manner, usually without urgency.

items.pt: aproximar-se de lado ou discretamente, às vezes com segundas intenções
items.example: The sales representative sidled up to the manager during the reception.
items.note: Approach obliquely and often furtively or ingratiatingly; may carry negative connotations.

items.pt: deslizar com suavidade; mover-se graciosamente
items.example: The skaters glided across the ice with hardly a sound.
items.note: Move smoothly and apparently effortlessly, without visibly heavy steps.

items.pt: circular de um lado para outro; ficar andando sem direção definida
items.example: Visitors milled around the lobby while waiting for the exhibition to open.
items.note: A group moves in different directions without a clear shared destination.

units.title: Unit 62 — Manner: behaviour and body language
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 130–131 (PDF pages 132–133).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · social behaviour and non-verbal signals
learningObjectives: Distinguish politeness, dismissiveness, insolence and conventional social etiquette.
Use singular manner and plural manners correctly in different contexts.
Interpret common body-language verbs and distinguish a warm smile from a self-satisfied one.
Recognise non-verbal expressions of embarrassment, fear, amusement, disgust and disapproval.

sectionsChecked: A · Manners and Language help on manner/manners
B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour table

items.pt: cortesia; educação; respeito no trato
items.example: Even under pressure, the receptionist treated every visitor with courtesy.
items.note: Politeness and consideration shown towards other people.

items.pt: cortês; educado e respeitoso
items.example: Her courteous response helped resolve a tense exchange.
items.note: Positive adjective describing respectful behaviour or speech.

items.pt: descortês; desrespeitoso
items.example: The review criticised the company's discourteous treatment of customers.
items.note: Formal adjective for conduct lacking politeness; generally less severe than insolent.

items.pt: desinteressado e brusco; pouco atencioso
items.example: His offhand reply made the applicant feel that the question had been dismissed.
items.note: Apparently dismissive or showing insufficient interest; not necessarily openly hostile.

items.pt: insolente; atrevido e desrespeitoso
items.example: The supervisor warned him about his insolent remarks to colleagues.
items.note: Strongly disrespectful or offensively rude, often towards someone in authority.

items.pt: etiqueta; regras de comportamento social
items.example: The induction session covered the etiquette of formal business dinners.
items.note: Socially accepted rules or customs for a particular setting or group.

items.pt: conservador nos costumes; moralmente rígido
items.example: Her straitlaced relatives disapproved of the unconventional wedding.
items.note: Having strict, traditional moral attitudes; usually mildly critical.

items.pt: etiqueta digital; boas maneiras na internet
items.example: Good netiquette includes acknowledging other contributors in online discussions.
items.note: Standards of considerate behaviour in online communication.

items.pt: boas maneiras; comportamento social
items.example: Good manners matter just as much in video meetings as in person.
items.note: The social-behaviour sense is normally plural: good manners, not good manner.

items.pt: maneira; modo de agir ou fazer algo
items.example: She explained the difficult news in a sensitive manner.
items.note: Singular manner means way or style, often more formal than way.

items.pt: fazer cerimônia; insistir em formalidades
items.example: Please don't stand on ceremony; help yourself to some tea.
items.note: Usually in negatives or invitations: not stand on ceremony means behave informally.

items.pt: o que é socialmente esperado ou considerado adequado
items.example: In that organisation, interrupting a senior colleague was not the done thing.
items.note: The customary or socially acceptable behaviour in a particular group.

items.pt: modos à mesa; etiqueta durante as refeições
items.example: Their children had excellent table manners even at formal gatherings.
items.note: Refers specifically to social behaviour when eating with others.

items.pt: linguagem corporal
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: Her body language suggested unease despite her reassuring words.
items.note: Meaning conveyed by posture, gesture, facial expression and movement.

items.pt: comunicação não verbal
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: Silence and non-verbal communication shaped the outcome of the negotiation.
items.note: Communication without spoken words; includes gestures, expressions and non-verbal sounds.

items.pt: erguer as sobrancelhas em sinal de surpresa ou desaprovação
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: The unusually high fee raised several committee members' eyebrows.
items.note: Shows surprise or scepticism; a person's behaviour can also raise eyebrows figuratively.

items.pt: contrair-se involuntariamente; ter um pequeno espasmo
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: His eyelid began to twitch after several sleepless nights.
items.note: Make small, often repeated involuntary movements, sometimes linked to nervousness.

items.pt: retrair-se bruscamente por dor, medo ou susto
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: She flinched when the dentist touched the sensitive tooth.
items.note: Make a sudden small movement in response to pain, fear or anticipated harm.

items.pt: remexer-se de desconforto; contorcer-se de vergonha
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: He squirmed in his chair as the interviewer questioned his earlier claim.
items.note: Move awkwardly from side to side through embarrassment, discomfort or nervousness.

items.pt: sorrir com presunção ou malícia; dar um sorriso de superioridade
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: He smirked as if the other team's mistake had proved his superiority.
items.note: A self-satisfied smile with negative implications, unlike beam.

items.pt: sorrir de orelha a orelha; irradiar alegria
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: Her parents beamed when she received the award.
items.note: Give a broad, delighted smile; positive rather than smug.

items.pt: demonstrar desdém ou reprovação por algo
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: Several reviewers sniffed at the proposal without examining the evidence.
items.note: Here sniff at expresses disdain or disapproval; not simply detecting a smell.

items.pt: bufar; soltar ar ruidosamente pelo nariz
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: The audience snorted with laughter at the unexpected punchline.
items.note: A sharp explosive nasal sound indicating amusement, disbelief or disgust depending on context.

items.pt: dar risadinhas nervosas ou constrangidas
items.section: B · Body language and non-verbal behaviour
items.example: A few people tittered when the speaker mispronounced the guest's name.
items.note: Laugh briefly and rather nervously or awkwardly, often less warmly than genuine laughter.
